A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Writing-RL. Their complete text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and added content.

before.justification: v1 reports original writing-benchmark evaluations, LongBench v2 generalization results, and experiments on data selection, rewards, reference quality, and curriculum scheduling.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds model configurations, human evaluations, general-capability benchmarks, judge-agreement measurements, and further ablations and analyses.

M1.justification: The three components, learning-potential formula, 1/0.5/0 comparison rewards, response ordering, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. GRPO and alternative judges are newly evaluated configurations of the existing framework; no revised framework procedure is specified.

E1.justification: v2 adds MMLU and MT-Bench evaluation, extending coverage to general knowledge and conversational capabilities beyond writing and long-context reasoning (Section 6.6, Table 6). The original training datasets and writing benchmarks remain; Creative-Writing-Bench is the renamed EQ-Bench creative-writing split.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Longwriter-Zero-32B and Reference-SFT comparators for both original model families, materially strengthening comparisons with existing writing RL and supervised training on the reference data. Appendix D.4 also adds a combined difficulty-prioritized selection and static-curriculum comparator. Existing main-table competitors are retained.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include 14B and GRPO configurations, alternative training-time judges, human preference evaluation on 100 prompts, and judge validation on 300 samples. Appendix D.3 adds a 1.2k selected-data condition alongside 1.5k and full-data conditions. Newly disclosed PPO/SFT parameters do not establish changes to previously reported runs.

E4.justification: v2 adds LongBench v2 component controls, instruction-overlap checks, output-length and failure analyses, judge and optimizer robustness tests, sample-size sensitivity, and reasoning and poetry case studies. The original component ablations remain. The scheduling illustration moved from v1 Figure 2 to v2 Figure 5 is retained evidence, not a new analysis.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. v2 newly reports three independent evaluation runs and mean/standard-deviation results in Tables 3–5, plus five-annotator majority voting and inter-annotator kappa of 0.69 in Appendix D.1. These additions quantify evaluation and annotation variability but do not establish additional independent training runs or seed robustness.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including averages of 88.53 for Qwen2.5-14B Writing-RL and 84.51 for the 7B GRPO configuration, human preferences, general-capability scores, and diagnostic results. Existing reported values also change: Table 1's Llama Writing-RL average changes from 87.40 to 87.29, and Table 3's margin-aware score from 87.02 to 86.98. These are reporting changes, not established same-setting performance improvements; Table 2's original generalization results are unchanged.

T1.justification: The learning-potential and reward definitions and scheduling algorithm are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added empirical analyses introduce no substantive mathematical derivation or formal result.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the underexplored research area from online outcome-based RL to adaptive online RL while acknowledging existing static-reward approaches. The performance contribution drops its explicit 7B restriction. The three-component contribution and the conclusion's output-to-input generalization claim remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C add interpretations attributing generalization primarily to RL, discussing data overlap, self-correction, and longer reasoning. v2 also adds interpretations concerning judge/optimizer independence, preservation of general capabilities, sample-size saturation, and cost-effectiveness. Appendix C.5 newly identifies the 32k context limit, missed details, and extended-reasoning failures as applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands reproducibility information with GAE parameters, critic initialization, rollout temperature, SFT optimizer and training settings, and itemized API and computational costs. Annotation procedures and guidance are also added. These are mainly new disclosures; existing prompts and the code link remain, while v1's explicit A100 hardware identification is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 adds LongWriter-Zero and MMLU references and removes the Wei et al. chain-of-thought citation. Its positioning now distinguishes adaptive curriculum RL from existing static-reward long-writing RL. Most related work remains unchanged after matching the renumbered Wu et al. citations.

P1.justification: v2 polishes and condenses existing prose, introduces result subheadings, standardizes benchmark terminology, and removes the duplicated curriculum-ablation paragraph and incorrect table references in v1 Section 6.4. Author information and appendix organization also change, but the main narrative and section sequence remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Table 1 is expanded and reorganized into labeled model groups, and component tables receive revised structures. New displays include human preferences, reasoning and poetry comparisons, and extensive control, agreement, distribution, and cost tables. The scheduling figure moves to Appendix D.2; the framework and original length-distribution figures are retained. Appendix prompt boxes are also restyled.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's empirical support through human preference evaluation, judge–human agreement, reference-data SFT comparisons, and controlled generalization analyses. New uncertainty reporting and implementation/cost details also improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the unexplained Llama average discrepancy between v2 Tables 1 and 17 and causal interpretations stronger than the controls establish.
